items.title: After Binance, check what your signing systems can approve
items.summary: Trail of Bits analyses Binance's October 2026 incident, in which an attacker compromised a wallet-signing service and used valid signatures rather than stolen keys. The attacker used an EIP-7702 delegation to install a standing instruction that allowed repeated transfers, including of later deposits, without further signatures. The article argues that monitoring must cover authority changes and delegation paths, not just transfers and ownership.
items.takeaway: A compromised server that can request signatures is as dangerous as a stolen private key, so detection must watch for new standing authority such as delegations and session keys, not only the asset movements they enable.

items.title: Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets
items.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed threat actors using an agentic AI framework, ARTEX, to scan public GitHub repositories for exposed credentials and AI API keys. In one case an agent went from finding a secret to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes. Follow-on activity involved service principal sign-ins using a compromised multitenant vendor application credential to reach downstream tenants.
items.takeaway: Exposed secrets are now found and exploited at machine speed, so rotate leaked credentials immediately and hunt for unusual service principal sign-ins, especially from multitenant application credentials.

items.title: Escalate or Close: How Fast-Tier Models Handle Held-Out Web Attack Families in Two-Tier Triage
items.summary: The study tests two-tier web attack triage where a fast model closes most requests, using seven attack families held out of all training and threshold tuning. Supervised detectors such as ModernBERT often give held-out path traversal confident benign scores, while hosted decision models escalate at least 97.6% of every family within the benign budget, though their training data is undisclosed. The authors also show that benign twin requests and scanner-like shapes can inflate apparent detection, and that a probability-guided search gets 43% of held-out attacks past one model within 300 queries
items.takeaway: Evaluate detectors on attack families they never saw, and include benign twins that share the attack's request shape, otherwise high scores may only reflect scanner-like structure or leaked training data.

items.title: Beyond Instruction Override: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injection with Task-Tampering Attacks
items.summary: The authors define indirect prompt injection by authority: planted content is an attack if it tries to influence a decision its source is not authorised to make, even when it does not issue an instruction. Their 90-case benchmark shows that attacks on decision rules, available actions, and state beliefs succeed more often than attacks on the objective, and that a detection-and-removal defence cuts objective attacks to 2.4% but leaves observation and state attacks at 9.5% and 12.1%. A tool-policy defence still allows 15.4% success, close to the 17.0% undefended rate.
items.takeaway: Prompt injection defences that only catch instruction-like text or block unexpected tools miss attacks that manipulate the values an agent reads during execution. Test defences against attacks that keep the expected task and tools but tamper with the decision inputs.

items.title: A Gingerbread House for LLM Agents: Source-Planned Honeypots That Lure Autonomous Attackers into an Isolated Shadow
items.summary: The authors have an LLM defender plan a static honeypot from application source code, then route confirmed attacker traffic, including working exploits, to an isolated shadow copy of the app. On 40 critical CVE-Bench tasks, real compromise fell from 26/40 to 5/40 for Claude Opus 4.8 and from 20/40 to 0/40 for the ARTEX attack framework. In about half the deception runs the exploit still worked, but against the shadow, and ARTEX accepted a planted fake secret as genuine in 30 of 120 deception-arm tasks.
items.takeaway: Deception can move an attacker's working exploit somewhere else rather than stop it, so defenders should measure whether the attack has been neutralised or only relocated. Requests that reach the real target before the attacker is identified remain the main exposure.

items.title: Signed but Not Safe: Requirement Integrity in Multi-Agent LLM Handoffs
items.summary: The authors test multi-agent LLM pipelines where an orchestrator passes requirements to subagents, comparing free-text, structured JSON and HMAC-signed requirement manifests. Signing sharply cut unsafe commits under attack and blocked in-transit tampering entirely, and a deterministic verifier outperformed an LLM checker on both detection and false alarms. However, a single adversarial line injected before signing was authenticated by the signature and raised violations sharply across three models.
items.takeaway: A signature only proves that data arrived unchanged, so the step that creates the data is the real trust boundary and needs its own controls.

items.title: SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection
items.summary: SPILLWAY is a runtime defence for tool-using agents that admits a tool call only when each new target value, such as an email recipient or payment account, came from a typed field returned by a read-only tool or matches a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitiser strips instruction-like text before the model reads it and keeps the removed spans as evidence. The authors report that no standard templated injection redirected an action to an attacker's target across three backbones and seven task suites, with mean in-scope attack success of 0.007 against a released reinforcement-learning a
items.takeaway: Where an agent sends data or money can often be enforced deterministically from the structure of tool outputs, rather than by asking a model to judge each action. Typed fields are harder to forge through free text than the content around them.

items.title: MEvince: Knowledge-Constrained LLM Reasoning for Technique Identification from Malware Reports
items.summary: MEvince is a framework that uses LLMs to map malware analysis reports to MITRE ATT&CK techniques, grounding the model in a shared behavioural representation built from technique documentation. It extracts observations linked to source passages, retrieves candidate techniques along with confusable alternatives, and checks evidence references before the LLM compares distinguishing behaviours. Across 610 public reports it improves exact-ID F1 by 17.4% over the strongest baseline and raises gold-label candidate coverage from 31.6% to 47.9%.
items.takeaway: When an LLM labels threat activity, require it to cite supporting evidence and to compare the closest confusable techniques, since plausible associations alone produce many false mappings. Retrieval coverage is often the bottleneck, so measure whether the correct answer is even among the candidates.

items.title: Detecting Silent Faults at the Environment-Trainer Boundary in Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: The authors treat the wire between a reinforcement learning trainer and its environment as a protocol and inject faults into it, including faults that raise no error. Learning-curve thresholds and comparisons with fault-free seeds caught very few faults, while a step ledger kept on both sides and compared step by step caught and located every fault that crossed. Several real faults were also found in Gymnasium and in multi-agent libraries.
items.takeaway: Check what the system actually did at each step, not just whether its final outcome looks plausible, because silent corruption can produce normal-looking results.

items.title: CANMentor: A Large-Small Model Collaboration Framework for CAN Bus Intrusion Detection
items.summary: The authors propose CANMentor, where a lightweight intrusion detector in each vehicle handles CAN bus traffic locally and a cloud LLM acts as a teacher, with a privacy-aware generator producing proxies so raw messages never leave the car. Teacher predictions are used only within a latency bound and are distilled back into the local model as soft targets. On non-IID partitions of the ROAD and HCRL Car-Hacking datasets, distillation gives up to 25.01% and 20.79% relative Macro F1 gains.
items.takeaway: When edge models are weak on skewed data, distilling soft targets from a stronger remote model can recover accuracy, but the design must also limit what sensitive data leaves the device and must have a fallback when the remote answer is late.

items.title: Fast Unsupervised Anomaly Detection Methods on Software Logs - An Empirical Study
items.summary: This empirical study tests unsupervised anomaly detection on software logs across seven datasets, including BGL, HDFS and Thunderbird, using four models and three text representations. Results vary widely by dataset, so no single recommendation holds everywhere, although training on anomaly-free data tends to help. The authors find that shuffling training data does not cause the leakage it causes for supervised models, and that word representations with models other than IsolationForest run fastest.
items.takeaway: Log anomaly detection results depend heavily on the dataset, so a detector tuned on one log source should be revalidated on yours before you trust its alerts.

items.title: The Promise of Strategic Agentic Scambaiting
items.summary: The paper presents a formal game-theoretic model of agent-to-agent fraud, in which scammer agents and scambaiting agents compete for each other's resources such as mule accounts and wallet addresses. Under the baseline parameters, scammer profitability turns negative once baiting-agent prevalence passes certain thresholds. When both sides improve at the same rate, the defender's gains in mimicry quality outpace the scammer's gains in detection, so the defender wins the arms race.
items.takeaway: In adversarial automation, the side that improves the realism of its deception may keep pace better than the side that improves detection. Model defensive value as a race over resource consumption and belief adaptation, not just as a detection accuracy problem.

items.title: JailBound: FOL-Guided Jailbreak Evaluation for Exploring LLM Behavioral Boundaries
items.summary: JailBound is a jailbreak evaluation framework that generates attack prompts across a taxonomy of threat conditions and uses a first-order loss signal to search for states near the boundary between refusal and unsafe output. Across 46 LLMs it reports modest attack success rate gains over a zeroth-order baseline and shows that local perturbations flip judged safety labels more often in sensitive states. The authors argue this gives a finer view of model behaviour than success rate alone.
items.takeaway: Attack success rate alone hides how fragile a model's refusal is, so measure how often small perturbations near the decision boundary flip its behaviour.

items.title: Req2Rust: A Requirements-Guided Agent Harness for Project-Level C++-to-Rust Migration
items.summary: Req2Rust is an LLM-based harness for project-level C++ to Rust migration. It first writes a Migration Requirements Specification of behaviours that must be preserved, then produces a Rust design and initial project, and refines the project using compiler, semantic, and unsafe-reduction validators. It produces buildable crates on general projects and OpenHarmony modules, raising test pass rates from 69.5% to 91.9% and from 45.4% to 87.9%.
items.takeaway: Migrating legacy code to a memory-safe language is more reliable when the behaviours to preserve are written down explicitly and checked by tests and validators. Treat the first generated translation as a starting point to refine, not as the final result.

items.title: SeVerus: Context-Aware, Gamified Benchmarking for Rust Verification
items.summary: SeVerus generates Verus benchmark tasks from real verified Rust projects by progressively removing the helper lemmas that originally supported each proof, arranged as gamified levels. A checker rejects weakened specifications and unsound proof constructs, and a noisy binary search estimates the hardest level an agent solves reliably. The strongest agent solved the final level of many quests yet reliably solved only about 35 percent of levels, with successful proofs often using different decompositions rather than the withheld lemmas.
items.takeaway: Benchmarks that supply the helper lemmas hide how much an agent can actually discover, so withholding context is a useful way to expose real capability gaps in verification tasks.
